How a span becomes a plan item

The target set is the model’s instrumented span manifest, so the plan is complete by construction: it cannot omit a behaviour the model implements, because every behaviour the model implements is compiled into a span. Four steps turn one into an item, each read from the sources rather than from a table.

StepWhat it recoversWhy it matters
Ownershipthe top-level definition containing the spanfunction clause execute RTYPE(...) owns its spans; so does pmpCheck. Cross-checked against the function names the compiler emitted — 99.9% agreement.
Discriminationthe enclosing match armInside an execute clause the model discriminates instructions by matching on the operand enum, so each arm is its own span. An uncovered span is not “an expression in RTYPE” — it is sra was never executed.
Namingthe arm’s assembly mnemonicThe model states it itself: SRA <-> "sra". Those mappings are unreachable as code and excluded from measurement, but they are the model’s own authority on what a constructor is called.
Stimuluswhat a generator must arrangeA guard on the span’s own line gives a privilege level, CSR field, configuration key or XLEN. A helper with no guard is resolved through the call graph to the instructions that reach it. Anything left is reported unclassified rather than guessed at.

Crosses

Two different things get called a cross, and the plan’s answer differs for each.

Operand-value crosses — not covered, and not coverable

ACT4’s cr_rs1_rs2_edges crosses 11 edge values on rs1 against 11 on rs2. None are visible here, because the model has no branch on operand values for arithmetic:

ADD  => X(rs1) + X(rs2),

That is one span, covered the first time any add executes, whatever the operands. All 121 combinations are indistinguishable to source coverage. This is a property of the metric, not a gap in the tooling, and it is why the RVVI/SVA coverpoints are measured alongside this plan rather than replaced by it.

Control-flow crosses — reported, with the conjunction

Where the model does branch on combinations, each span carries its full chain of enclosing conditions, not just the nearest — a directive naming only the innermost sends the generator after a state it will never reach. 916 spans (6.1%) need two or more conditions to hold together; 301 are uncovered.

DepthSpansShareUncovered
unconditional11,21574.9%2,313
one condition2,84419.0%1,552
two at once7054.7%184
three at once1761.2%101
four or more350.2%16
On the depth figure. } else if c then { is an alternative, not a nesting — exactly one of the chain holds, never all of them. Counting those as nesting put clint_store at depth 8 and claimed eight conditions had to hold simultaneously. A line’s leading } is applied before its {, so an else-if chain stays at constant depth.

What is excluded, and on what basis

Two kinds of “cannot be reached” are kept apart, because they justify different things. The distinction is what keeps the headline figure honest: the plan is allowed to say do not schedule this, and not allowed to say so it does not count.

KindItemsDenominatorBasis
Held unreachable325removedWhole declaration forms reasoned about structurally by derive_span_exclusions.py: the disassembly direction of a bidirectional mapping is not reachable by running a program, for any such mapping.
Out of reach53retainedDecided per span from its own text: enum-to-text mappings in another declaration form, diagnostic string builders, and Hypervisor code the model does not implement. A per-span judgement is not a strong enough basis to move a coverage figure, so these are excluded from the schedule but not deducted.

Reproducing this

cd python-isla
python3 derive_span_exclusions.py -o /tmp/excl.txt
python3 testplan.py \
    --coverage ~/Documents/sail-riscv/sail_coverage \
    --exclude-spans /tmp/excl.txt \
    --baseline documentation/python-isla/results/testplan.json \
    -o testplan --html --xlsx --fail-on-new-holes

Stale inputs stop the run rather than producing a plausible plan: a manifest older than the model would describe the previous model, and a coverage log older than the manifest would join status onto spans that have since moved. --baseline separates new holes and regressions from the standing backlog, and --fail-on-new-holes exits non-zero on either, so a model bump fails CI rather than quietly enlarging the backlog.
